title: Who owns this address? Lookalike domains
body_md:
## Whose gate is the sign on?

You are in the queue at the pharmacy when an SMS arrives. Your Harbor Bank card has been frozen, it says, and the link to unlock it begins with the bank’s own name. Your thumb is already moving. Hold it for a second. A familiar name inside a link tells you who the sender would like to be, not who owns the address. What this lesson trains is one habit: find the **host**, the part that says where the page really lives, and decide whether the request deserves a check somewhere else. It slows a rushed decision down. It does not certify a page as safe.

A URL has a scheme (`https://`), an authority that contains the host, and then a path. Take `https://accounts.harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net/verify`, an invented address. The host is `accounts.harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net`, and the bank-shaped text on the left is only a subdomain. Whoever controls `example.net` (in this invented address, the scammer) can put any words they like in front of it, the way anyone can screw a brass plate reading “Harbor Bank” to their own garden gate. The authority ends before `/`, `?`, `#` or the end of the URL. The host leaves out anything before an `@` (user information) and any port after a `:`. A bank’s name in the path, in the query or on the logo of the page is weaker evidence still. When an address is knotty, hand it to a proper URL parser, and check the request itself some other way.

## Counting dots will not save you

In `login.harborbank.co.uk` the public suffix is `co.uk`, so the part you can register is `harborbank.co.uk`: **three** labels. For a typical `.com` name it is two. Some suffixes are longer still, and private hosting services draw boundaries of their own. The [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/learn/) records these rules; no count-the-dots shortcut replaces it. And even a correctly parsed registrable domain tells you only who may control the address. It does not show that the request is authorised, that the account is secure or that the site has not been broken into.

## One wrong character

A lookalike can change the label right before the suffix. The digit `0` in the invented `harb0rbank.example` is not the letter `o` in `harborbank.example`. The `.example` suffix is reserved for documentation, so these are illustrations and not live bank addresses. Domain names may also contain letters from other alphabets, and some of them look just like Latin ones. Browsers and registries guard against this in different ways, so you cannot count on your screen to expose every confusable character, or on your eye to catch it. [ICANN explains how homograph attacks work](https://www.icann.org/en/announcements/details/icann-statement-on-idn-homograph-attacks-and-request-for-public-comment-23-2-2005-en). An odd character is a reason to stop and check. It is no proof that every name in another script is malicious.

## Four things to do with a link you do not trust

1. Pause before you open it. If it matters, go to the service from a bookmark, its installed app or an address you already know. Pasting the suspect link into the address bar “to check it” is just opening it.
2. If you do inspect the URL, separate the host from the path and from anything before an `@`, then read the whole spelling, letter by letter. A padlock or HTTPS means the connection can be encrypted. It says nothing about who is at the other end.
3. A short link, a QR code, a phone preview and a cramped address bar all show you part of the story. Ask for the full destination or take your own road. A brand logo or a familiar-looking subdomain proves nothing.
4. A genuine organisation sometimes works through a contractor or a regional domain you have never seen. That calls for confirmation through its known app, its website or its published support channel. It does not call for an instant “scam” verdict, or for a click to find out.

If you have already typed a password or a one-time code, leave the page, open the real service by your own route, change the affected password, review active sessions and multi-factor sign-in (MFA), and contact the provider through its usual support channel. Reading a URL can prevent a mistake. It does not replace the work that follows one.

widget_config.goal: Faced with a suspicious link, find its host, catch a lookalike character, and choose a route of your own for checking before you type anything.

blocks.title: A bank’s name on a stranger’s host
blocks.situation: Between two meetings an SMS arrives. Harbor Bank has frozen your card, it says, and the unlock link is https://harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net/unlock. The sender name looks right, too.
blocks.analysis: Read the host from the right: harborbank.co.uk.case-review.example.net. In this example example.net is the part the scammer registered, and the bank’s name is only a subdomain in front of it, which says nothing about who owns the address. Type nothing into that link. Open the bank’s app yourself and look at the card there.

blocks.title: Unfamiliar does not mean fake
blocks.situation: Your bank’s app, opened from your phone’s home screen, says your new card is being delivered by a partner at tracking.harbor-delivery.co.uk. A separate SMS mentions the same address.
blocks.analysis: The spelling cannot tell you whether this partner is real. The app you opened yourself can, and here it is your trusted cross-check. Follow its own handoff or its support route, and do not treat the SMS as verified just because the two match. On the domain itself: under the public suffix co.uk, the registrable part is harbor-delivery.co.uk, not co.uk.

blocks.title: One character changes the bank’s name
blocks.situation: A message offers a bank sign-in at harb0rbank.example. On a small screen the zero can pass for the o in Harbor Bank.
blocks.analysis: The digit 0 and the letter o are different characters, and the swap sits in the label right before the reserved .example suffix, the spot where a registrant’s own name would go under a real suffix. This address is a harmless illustration, but a real lookalike would have none of the bank’s authority behind it. Do not test one with a password. Open the known bank app or a saved address and check the claim there. Similar-looking Unicode letters set the same trap, although names in other scripts are used honestly too.

blocks.title: A delivery alert that wants your bank login
blocks.setup: An invented scenario. An SMS says delivery of your new card is on hold. The link has a bank name in it, and you are told to confirm your login before 18:00. Take the decisions in order.

steps.prompt: The message shows https://harborbank.co.uk.card-status.example.net/confirm. What do you take from the address?

choices.text: The bank’s name is right there in the link, so it belongs to the bank.
choices.consequence: You are ready to type your password into a site nobody has vouched for.
choices.explanation: Those words are only the beginning of a host that ends in example.net.

choices.text: The host ends in example.net; the bank’s name in front of it proves nothing.
choices.consequence: You stop before the sign-in form opens.
choices.explanation: In this invented .net address, example.net is the registrable part, and the bank-shaped words are a subdomain under it.

choices.text: The link is HTTPS and the padlock will show, so it must be the bank.
choices.consequence: You trust an encrypted line that runs to a stranger.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection to the host. It does not say who runs the host.

steps.prompt: You open the page. The bank logo is flawless, and you have typed nothing. What now?

choices.text: Close the tab and open the bank’s app yourself.
choices.consequence: You stop before any detail leaves your phone, and you check the claim somewhere you know.
choices.explanation: A page can look however its owner likes, so it authenticates nothing. The app is a separate road.

choices.text: Type just your username, to see whether the page recognises you.
choices.consequence: A stranger now holds an identifier for your account.
choices.explanation: Even half a login is something an attacker can use. Stop, and check outside the page.

choices.text: Click the logo and judge the site by its home page.
choices.consequence: You are still wandering round a site nobody has verified.
choices.explanation: Clicking around inside a site does not show who controls it.

steps.prompt: A second link in the message is https://login.harborbank.co.uk/account. Which claim about its domain is sound?

choices.text: The registrable part is co.uk, because it is always the last two labels.
choices.consequence: You draw the boundary in the wrong place on a co.uk name.
choices.explanation: co.uk is the public suffix; here the registrable part is harborbank.co.uk.

choices.text: The registrable part is harborbank.co.uk, though that alone does not validate the request.
choices.consequence: You keep the clue about who owns the address apart from whether you trust this message.
choices.explanation: The Public Suffix List treats co.uk as a suffix. The request still needs checking another way.

choices.text: Any co.uk link is safe, because UK domains are regulated.
choices.consequence: You skip the check on a false assumption.
choices.explanation: A suffix says nothing about who sent a link or why.

steps.prompt: The SMS shortens a third link, and your phone’s preview hides most of the address. What do you do next?

choices.text: Open the short link and judge the page by its logo.
choices.consequence: A convincing page could collect your login before you know where you are.
choices.explanation: A logo and a short link reveal nothing about who controls the host.

choices.text: Open the bank app from your home screen and check the delivery there, or ask support.
choices.consequence: You learn the true state of your account without following the message.
choices.explanation: Your own road breaks the chain from message to login.

choices.text: Forward the SMS to a friend and ask what they make of it.
choices.consequence: The link travels on, and you still have no authoritative answer.
choices.explanation: A friend can help you think. Only the bank’s app or its published support channel can confirm what is happening with your card.

steps.prompt: Suppose you had already typed your password before you noticed the address. What now?

choices.text: Nothing; the page used HTTPS.
choices.explanation: HTTPS does not stop the site’s operator from keeping what you typed.

choices.text: Through the real app or a known website, change the password, review active sessions and MFA, and contact support.
choices.consequence: You start cutting off possible access, using a channel you trust.
choices.explanation: Changing the exposed credential and checking account activity answers the exposure itself.

choices.text: Reply to the SMS and ask the sender to delete your password.
choices.consequence: You are still relying on the same unverified contact.
choices.explanation: Whoever took the password will not tidy up after themselves.

blocks.debrief: The order to keep: pause, find the host if you can see it, verify by a road you already know, and act quickly if you have already handed something over. A registrable domain is one clue, not a verdict, and a suspect link is never tested by typing into it. If your first answer was wrong, the page that opened gave you a second chance to stop before entering anything, and its polish still proved nothing. Go back and take another branch.

questions.prompt: In https://help.example.co.uk/login, what does the co.uk part show?

choices.text: The registrable part can be example.co.uk, so a fixed rule of two labels fails.
choices.explanation: co.uk is a public suffix, so the label in front of it belongs to the registrable name.

choices.text: The registrable part has to be co.uk.
choices.explanation: co.uk is the public suffix, not a name this site registered.

choices.text: Any address with three or more labels is malicious.
choices.explanation: Honest sites use subdomains and multi-label suffixes all the time.

questions.prompt: What does the HTTPS padlock establish about a login page?

choices.text: That the login request really came from the service named in the message.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not authenticate who sent the message.

choices.text: That the connection to that host can be protected, though the operator may still be untrustworthy.
choices.explanation: Encryption protects the line, not the operator. Check the request through a route you already know.

questions.prompt: An unfamiliar delivery partner shows up inside an app you opened yourself. What should you do?

choices.text: Treat the partner as fake because you do not know the domain.
choices.explanation: Genuine services do use partners. Confirm the handoff inside the app you trust.

choices.text: Confirm through the app’s own handoff or support, and go on only if it matches.
choices.explanation: An app you opened yourself gives you more context than the SMS does.

choices.text: Use the link in the SMS, since it names the same partner.
choices.explanation: The SMS link stays unverified even when it repeats a real partner’s name.

questions.prompt: A URL contains bank.example.com@signin.example.net. What is the host?

choices.text: bank.example.com
choices.explanation: Text before the @ is user information inside the authority, not the host.

choices.text: signin.example.net
choices.explanation: The host follows the @ and ends at a slash, a question mark, a hash sign or the end of the URL.

questions.prompt: An invented message shows harb0rbank.example rather than harborbank.example. What follows from that?

choices.text: One changed character is harmless if the page has HTTPS.
choices.explanation: HTTPS can encrypt a connection to the wrong host. It does not mend the spelling.

choices.text: Any domain with letters from other alphabets is fraudulent.
choices.explanation: Such names are used honestly too, and appearance alone is no verdict.

choices.text: Treat the spelling as a warning, and check the request in the known bank app or at a saved address.
choices.explanation: The zero changes the label right before the reserved .example suffix. In a real registered name that could point to a different owner, so use a route of your own and enter no credentials.

widget_config.today_action: Save your bank, or any service that holds real money, as a bookmark you trust, or make sure its genuine app is installed. The next time a message pushes you towards a link, take that route instead and check the request there.
widget_config.scope: General guidance on reading URLs. Harbor Bank and every address in the examples are invented. Public suffix rules follow the current list, and what to do after an exposure differs by service and country.

sources.title: Public Suffix List: Learn
sources.scope: Why co.uk and other public suffixes make a fixed count of labels unreliable.

sources.title: MDN: URI authority
sources.scope: What counts as the host, and what as user information, inside a URL’s authority.

sources.title: UK NCSC: Phishing scams
sources.scope: General advice on checking a suspicious message through channels you already trust; the reporting routes are UK-only.

sources.title: ICANN: IDN homograph attacks
sources.scope: How lookalike letters, within ASCII and across scripts, fool the eye. The statement dates from 2005 and does not describe how each browser shows addresses today.

sources.title: IANA: Special-Use Domain Names
sources.scope: Confirms that .example and its subdomains are reserved for examples, so none of them is a live service address.
